Nothing is good in itself, and nothing is evil in itself.
Something is good because revealed law declares it good by praising the person who does it. Something is evil because revealed law declares it evil by condemning the person who does it.
At the same time, revelation does not praise, blame, command, or prohibit something because the thing itself already possesses an inherent quality of good or evil.
For this reason, reason has no independent authority to judge that one thing or action is good and another is bad.

One of the Ashʿarite arguments for this view is that if goodness and badness belonged objectively to a thing itself, then whatever was good would always be good, and whatever was bad would always be bad. Neither quality would depend on any conditions.
But in reality, they say, good and bad are not absolute. They are relative.
The same thing may be good in one situation and bad in another.
Killing, for example, is bad when the person killed has committed no crime deserving death. But it may be good when it is carried out as just punishment for a crime.
If good and evil existed objectively in the thing itself, their character could not change with circumstances.
Likewise, the same thing may be good at one time and not good at another.

Revealed laws themselves prescribe one thing for one people and something different for another. If good and evil existed objectively within things themselves, religious laws would not change with time, place, and people.
This Ashʿarite argument is right in one respect and weak in another.
It is right in saying that good and evil are relative rather than absolute.

But how can we judge, before revealed law appears, that killing in one case is good and in another bad? And how do we decide that a truth which helps someone is good, while a truth which harms someone is bad? What standard are we using?

In making this argument, the Ashʿarites themselves were admitting that good and bad have an objective, though relative, basis in things. Yet they did not show that reason is incapable of recognizing this relative good and bad. So they could not overturn the Muʿtazilite position at its foundation, because reason is the very basis of that position.

Besides, the Muʿtazilites themselves never said that things were good or bad in some absolute sense. Their position can instead be understood like this: killing as just retribution is good in itself, while unjust killing is bad in itself; telling a truth that helps is good in itself, while telling a truth that causes harm is bad in itself, and so on. In other words, what they judged good or bad was not simply “killing,” “truth,” or “lying” in the abstract. It was just killing or unjust killing, helpful truth-telling or harmful truth-telling, and the same applies to lying.

There are also things such as injustice, where we can identify a relatively fixed basis for judging them bad. The same is true of justice when we judge it good. Injustice remains injustice regardless of changes in people, circumstances, or periods of history. Justice likewise remains justice. The Ashʿarite argument does not cover acts of this kind, whose goodness or badness reason can recognize in themselves whether or not religious law has spoken about them.
Some Ashʿarites added another argument. They said that our judgments about what is good or bad come either from earlier religious laws or from human customs and conventions:

“Suppose a person were created with a sound nature and a complete mind, but had never acquired the morals of any people, learned the manners of his parents, received a religious upbringing, or been taught by a teacher. Then suppose two propositions were put before him. The first: two is greater than one. The second: lying is bad. He would have no hesitation about the first, but he would hesitate about the second.

“What remains, then, is simply the custom by which people call whatever harms them bad and whatever benefits them good. We do not deny the use of such names. But they differ from one people to another, from one period to another, from one place to another, and according to different relationships and circumstances. Anything that varies with such relationships and circumstances cannot have an intrinsic reality of its own. One people may consider the slaughter of an animal good while another considers it bad. The same act may be good for one people, in one time and place, and bad in another.”
And: “Reasonable people approve of saving those who are drowning and condemn aggression because they seek praise and fear blame.”
What we said about the Ashʿarites’ first argument also applies here. But two further points can be added.
First, the Muʿtazilite position assumes that there was a time before divine laws had been revealed.
Second, human customs themselves must rest on some rational judgment that one thing is good and another bad. Customs do not simply appear at random, with no basis in human understanding.

It seems that later Ashʿarites became aware of this weakness in their argument against the Muʿtazila. The author of al-Mawāqif reports them as saying that there is actually no disagreement between the Ashʿarites and the Muʿtazila when the words “good” and “bad” refer to perfection and deficiency in a thing. We can say, for example, that knowledge is good and ignorance is bad, and both sides agree that reason can recognize this.

The same words can also refer to what serves a purpose and what does not, or to what brings benefit and what causes harm. In this sense, whatever serves the purpose or brings benefit is good, while whatever frustrates the purpose or causes harm is bad. Here too, there is no disagreement that reason can recognize the difference, even though the judgment is relative. Something may be good for one group and bad for another in this sense.

The real disagreement, they say, concerns whether an action deserves praise and reward, or blame and punishment. The Muʿtazila say that reason can judge this too, and that we can therefore judge some actions deserving of blame and punishment. Their opponents say that this can only be known through revealed law.
What can we conclude from this?

The strength of Muʿtazilite reasoning, together with the steady development of intellectual debate toward greater reliance on reason, gradually narrowed the disagreement between the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites on this issue. The same happened in other areas as well. Despite their deep differences in principles, assumptions, and starting points, rational argument increasingly became the dominant method in both schools.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

We have discussed many of the questions in these two chapters at great length, sometimes in considerable detail. This was not accidental, nor did we simply allow ourselves to drift into one digression after another. It was part of the plan from the beginning.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Our aim was to reach an important conclusion.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The emergence of philosophical thought among the Arabs, and its later development from the historical period in which it first appeared, did not take place apart from the internal development of Arab-Islamic society in its economic, social, political, and cultural life.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This brings us back to a point we made when we began our discussion of atomism. During the period in which the Muʿtazila emerged, Arab thought—and Arab culture more broadly—was certainly influenced by philosophical ideas, theories, and schools that came from outside. But this influence worked from within. Foreign ideas entered an internal process that was closely and objectively connected with the laws governing the social, intellectual, and religious development of Arab-Islamic life.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

After examining many of the disputes between the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites, and also the disagreements among the leading Muʿtazilite thinkers themselves, we can now return to the idea we introduced at the start of our study of atomism: the process of “fusion and transformation.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

By this we meant that philosophical ideas, theories, and schools from many different foreign sources were drawn into the internal current of Arab-Islamic intellectual life, a current that often moved with great force. Within it, those ideas were fused and transformed until they became an integral and original part of Arab-Islamic thought itself.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This is how that thought acquired its own distinctive character and became noticeably independent of the foreign sources from which many of these ideas, theories, and concepts had originally come.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

In every disputed question we examined, whether it concerned purely divine matters or the natural world and human society, the basic starting points were Islamic. But they did not come from Islamic metaphysics considered in the abstract. They came from the real relationship between Islam and the lives of the people among whom its concepts took concrete form—in economic, social, and political systems, and in forms of culture and thought.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

There is no doubt that cultural and social interaction between these people and the cultures and inherited civilizations of other peoples was one of the powerful forces driving change. During the historical period in which the Muʿtazila appeared, this interaction helped give development a new pace and a new character.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But interaction is not the same thing as mere passive influence.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Interaction takes place between two sides and produces a qualitative change in both.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

That is exactly what happened when Arab thought in this period came into contact with the intellectual heritage of the Greeks, Indians, Persians, and Christians, as well as the wider cultural and civilizational traditions of the peoples whom the Arabs encountered in many different ways after the rise of Islam.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This interaction produced a qualitative change not only in Arab thought. It also had a major effect on the direction of philosophical and scientific thought in other parts of the world, especially once its mature results began to appear from the twelfth century onward.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

At the same time, it changed the cultures of the peoples who formed the other side of this interaction. Here we mean the non-Arab peoples across wide areas of Asia and Africa who adopted Islam, whether as a religious faith or simply as a social and political system.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

One sign of this qualitative change is that many of the Muʿtazilite thinkers and their opponents during the period when philosophical thinking began to emerge were themselves not of Arab origin. The same is true of many later philosophers who came to represent the distinctive character of Arab philosophical thought. They came from peoples living across the eastern lands stretching from India and Persia to the regions south and north of the Caucasus, Asia Minor, Central Asia, North Africa, and the rest of the Maghreb.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
All of this is very different from saying that Arab-Islamic thought merely received foreign intellectual and philosophical influences.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
To describe the relationship as mere passive influence is to make Arab-Islamic thought a follower: something that copies and transmits rather than creates.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Yet in the previous chapter we saw ideas, theories, and concepts among both the Muʿtazila and their opponents that had indeed been influenced by similar ideas among Greek, Indian, and other philosophers. At the same time, however, we saw that Muʿtazilite thinkers approached these foreign ideas from within their own social and ideological setting. That setting, within Arab-Islamic society, formed the root and foundation even of the internal workings of Muʿtazilite thought itself.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The Muʿtazilite relationship with the cultures around it was therefore one of internal and objective fusion and transformation. It did not depend on a deliberate mechanical process of accepting some ideas and rejecting others, nor on an artificial act of picking and choosing.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

On this basis, we can say that the Muʿtazila absorbed from these cultures whatever enabled them to deepen their own ideas about the two principles of divine unity and divine justice, as they understood them within their own Islamic and Muʿtazilite framework.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“Absorption” here means something much broader than acceptance or rejection. In fact, it makes that distinction almost meaningless. It means taking in the whole body of intellectual material available in these cultures, whether it agreed with Islamic ideology or contradicted it.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This is why, throughout our discussion of Muʿtazilite questions in the previous two chapters, we repeatedly found that even the ideas, theories, and concepts they drew from outside were changed in the process. Sometimes they were developed further. In every case, they were made to serve the Muʿtazila’s own basic direction and starting points, both in doctrine and in method.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
That, in itself, is an act of intellectual creation.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
One example is Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf’s discussion of the divine attributes, one of the questions connected with the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

As we saw, when discussing the unity of God’s essence and arguing that the attributes and the essence are one rather than many, he said that God is knowing through a knowledge that is His essence, powerful through a power that is His essence, and living through a life that is His essence.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
What he means is that God’s essence is knowledge, power, and life. These qualities are not something separate from the divine essence. They are the essence itself.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Al-Shahrastānī says that this view was borrowed from philosophers “who held that His essence is one and contains no multiplicity of any kind, and that the attributes are not meanings existing beyond the essence and residing in it; rather, they are the essence itself.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Al-Shahrastānī then says: “If Abū al-Hudhayl establishes these attributes as aspects of the essence, then they are exactly the hypostases of the Christians.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Dr. Jamīl Ṣalībā, meanwhile, says that Abū al-Hudhayl’s view “resembles Plato’s claim that the highest good is intellect, life, and soul, because knowledge comes through intellect and power through soul. It also resembles what the philosophers of Alexandria said about the three principles: the One, Intellect, and Soul.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

If it is true that Abū al-Hudhayl borrowed his view from philosophers—meaning here the Islamic philosophers—or from the Christian doctrine of the hypostases, or especially from Plato, or from the philosophers of Alexandria, he still gave the question a form of his own.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

He began from the specifically Muʿtazilite understanding of divine unity. He did not simply adopt those earlier theories as they stood, nor did he accept their philosophical direction apart from his own Islamic and Muʿtazilite starting point.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Our study of Muʿtazilite thought has shown that the Muʿtazila were so committed to reason that this commitment sometimes came close to outweighing their adherence to certain established principles of Islam.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
They made reason the judge that could move Qurʾānic texts away from their apparent meaning whenever that meaning conflicted with what reason required.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We even saw them make human freedom of choice take priority over the freedom of God’s will and, in this sense, place a limit on divine power.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Because their principle of human freedom necessarily depended on the existence of reason. And reason itself would have no meaning unless human beings also possessed the power to choose. Without reason and choice, people could not be held responsible for their actions, and divine justice would no longer be truly just.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Reason, then, stands at the center of this entire system.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The same is true of their theory of knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

For the Muʿtazila, there were almost no limits to the reach of reason, either in the natural world or beyond it. Even knowledge of God was not merely within reason’s reach. It was reason’s first necessary duty and, indeed, one of its most basic forms of knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
There was therefore no question in existence that the human mind was completely incapable of understanding in some way.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Even sensory knowledge fell within the work of reason in two ways.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
First, things perceived by the senses were themselves objects of rational knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Second, reason was what transformed sensory perceptions into rational understanding.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Many earlier and modern scholars have thought that the Muʿtazila went too far in extending the authority of reason.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
One modern scholar, however, found the reason for this apparent excess in what he described as something like “a reaction to the state of certain doctrines in their time.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

He explained that the Muʿtazila “affirmed the authority of reason, and exaggerated it, in the face of people who recognized no authority for reason at all. These people said: we stop at the text. Where the text is clear and decisive, we follow it. Where it is ambiguous or obscure, we leave its meaning to God.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

He explained their insistence on freedom of choice in the same way. They “went to an extreme in defending it because they faced people who stripped human beings of all will, making a person like a feather blown by the wind or a piece of wood tossed in the sea.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
In this scholar’s view, “error in affirming the authority of reason and freedom of will, even when taken too far, is better than going too far in denying them.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“If the Muʿtazilite teachings on these two matters—the authority of reason and freedom of will—had prevailed among Muslims from the age of the Muʿtazila until today, Muslims would have occupied a very different place in history from the one they occupy now. Submission has left them powerless, determinism has paralyzed them, and passive dependence has held them back.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

In our view, this is a sound and realistic explanation of the Muʿtazilite position on reason and human freedom of will, despite the author’s description of that position as excessive or extreme. That description itself comes from a cautious, even conservative, view of the issue.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But his explanation deals only with the immediate intellectual side of the question. It does not address the social dimension that we uncovered earlier in our discussion of the Qadarites.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
His final comment, however, leads us to a conclusion that we consider extremely important: the historical value of the Muʿtazila’s insistence on reason in that period.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Their firm and courageous defence of reason helped, in our view, to drive intellectual life rapidly and far into new areas of rational and philosophical inquiry.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
In doing so, it helped prepare the ground not only for the coming philosophical period but also for the later rise of scientific activity, both in breadth and in depth.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

By opening so many fields of knowledge to rational inquiry, the Muʿtazila helped create the strong intellectual foundation needed for the later development of philosophy and science on the wide scale that would characterize the Arab-Islamic world for at least four centuries.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Ahmed Amin’s explanation also helps us understand a second point.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

It shows how deeply Muʿtazilite thought was connected with the wider intellectual life of its own society and period, and with the many competing positions people were taking on the major questions of that society.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This is what Ahmed Amin means when he says that the Muʿtazilite position on reason “was unavoidable, because it was something like a reaction to the state of certain doctrines in their time.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
And this is another example of the point we stressed in the previous section: the process of fusion and transformation.
